Carpets In Quadri 2

GeometryAreaConstructions
Game: This is a picture, not a game: four little corner pieces have exactly the same total area as the middle piece.
How to play: Drag the corners A, B, C and D, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the two cuts, the names of the points, or to hide a cut.
Look for the math

Drag a corner of the quadrilateral and the coloured pieces change shape. Yet the four corner pieces always add up to exactly the piece in the middle. Bui Quang Tuan suggested this puzzle; Bogomolny called it a carpet because two coloured carpets are laid over the same floor.

Two carpets, one floor

Let E, F, G, H be the midpoints of AB, BC, CD, DA. Tick only Partition 1: the blue shape AFCH is one half of the whole, and the two red triangles ABF and CDH make the other half. Tick only Partition 2: the blue shape BGDE is a half too, and the red triangles ADE and BCG are the other half. For example, [ADE] = [BDE] because E is the middle of AB, and [BCG] = [BDG] because G is the middle of CD; adding gives [ADE] + [BCG] = [BGDE].

The overlapping pieces

Where the blue halves overlap lies the four-sided shape PQRS: P is where AF meets DE, Q is where AF meets BG, R is where BG meets CH, and S is where CH meets DE. Where the red halves overlap lie the four corner triangles AEP, BFQ, CGR and DHS. The area of each whole carpet equals the area of its complement, so the Carpet Theorem says those two overlaps have equal area:

[AEP] + [BFQ] + [CGR] + [DHS] = [PQRS]

The logic test checks this on the starting shape, on squares, rectangles, tilted shapes, parallelograms and thousands of generated convex quadrilaterals: the two sides agree to machine precision every time. Make a shape with a dent in it and the equality can fail — the puzzle is about convex quadrilaterals.

How this differs from the first carpet

In Carpets in a Quadrilateral you slide two points P and Q along the sides AB and CD at the same fraction of the way, and compare the middle shape PSQR with just two red triangles, ARD and BSC. Here all four points are fixed at the middles of the four sides, so four corner triangles appear instead of two, and the middle shape is PQRS. The partition boxes let you lay down either carpet alone or both at once, which is how the proof becomes visible.

The one-fifth remark

The original page adds that a square leaves a middle square with 1/5 of its area, and says this carries over because any convex quadrilateral is an affine image of a square. That last sentence is not right: an affine transformation sends a square to a parallelogram, so the fifth is guaranteed only there. The logic test confirms that parallelograms give [PQRS] = [ABCD]/5 exactly, while a skewed convex shape such as A(0,0), B(100,0), C(80,20), D(0,60) gives about 0.195. The carpet equality itself still holds for every convex shape.

Tick one partition box at a time, then both: the middle piece is where the two blue halves overlap, and the corner pieces are where the two red halves overlap.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
